I'll systematically work through the immune response layer, applying the P-pass falsification loop to identify what the 50 prior findings missed.

**FINDING_ID: IM_F001**
SEVERITY: 0.88
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.82
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `_verify_remediation_outcomes` never checks whether the escalated `chain_idx` exceeds the length of the remediation chain before writing it back into `_remediation_state`. When a remediation is INEFFECTIVE, the code does `state["chain_idx"] += 1` and updates `applied_round` and `metric_at_apply` — but it never validates that `chain_idx + 1` is a valid index in `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS[pathology_key]`. CC2_IM_F017 identified the "zombie entry" aspect (entry can never be cleared), but missed the deeper issue: the next call to `apply_diagnosis()` will attempt to index into the chain with an out-of-bounds index. The caller `apply_diagnosis()` uses `health_monitor.recommended_chain_start(key)` which can also return an out-of-bounds index (CC2_IM_F002), but even when `recommended_chain_start` returns a valid index, `_verify_remediation_outcomes` can independently push `chain_idx` past the chain length between rounds. These are two independent paths to the same out-of-bounds access, and neither calls `record_chain_exhaustion()` to signal that the chain is spent. The verification loop will keep re-verifying the zombie entry every `verification_window` rounds, each time incrementing `chain_idx` further, producing an infinite sequence of INEFFECTIVE diagnoses with monotonically increasing (and meaningless) chain indices.
PROPOSED_FIX: After `state["chain_idx"] += 1`, check `if state["chain_idx"] >= len(self._REMEDIATION_CHAINS.get(pathology_key, []))`. If true, call `self.record_chain_exhaustion(pathology_key)`, delete the entry from `_remediation_state`, and emit a CRITICAL diagnosis instead of the escalation diagnosis.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F002**
SEVERITY: 0.85
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.85
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `record_round()` and `record_model_round()` have no ordering contract, but the immune layer's correctness depends on `record_model_round()` being called BEFORE `record_round()` for each round. `record_round()` calls `_verify_remediation_outcomes()` and `self_diagnose()`, both of which read `_model_finding_history`, `_model_failure_counts`, and `_model_response_times` — all populated by `record_model_round()`. If `record_round()` is called first (which is natural since it takes aggregate metrics), the verification and self-diagnosis operate on stale per-model data from the previous round. The interface summary shows `process_round()` calls both, but the artifact doesn't show the call order. The methods have no guard (e.g., checking that per-model data for the current round exists), no documentation of the ordering requirement, and no mechanism to enforce it. This is a temporal coupling bug: two methods that appear independent have a hidden sequencing dependency.
PROPOSED_FIX: Either (a) merge `record_model_round` data collection into `record_round` by accepting per-model data as a parameter, or (b) add a round-index parameter to both methods and have `record_round` assert that all expected model rounds have been recorded for that index, or (c) document the ordering contract as a HARD precondition with a runtime check.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F003**
SEVERITY: 0.82
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.75
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `self_diagnose()` Self-check 1 gates on `current_round < 5` to avoid premature self-assessment, but `remediation_success_rate` uses a rolling window of the last 10 outcomes regardless of when they occurred. If 3 remediations all fail in rounds 5-6 (early in the protocol), `success_rate` drops to 0.0 and triggers window widening. But the sample size is 3 — far too small for a reliable rate estimate. The `len(self._remediation_outcomes) >= 3` check is the only guard, and 3 is statistically insufficient to distinguish a 30% true rate from a 0% observed rate (binomial CI at n=3, k=0 is [0%, 70.8%] at 95% confidence). The self-adjustment then widens detection windows based on noise, potentially masking real pathologies for the remainder of the protocol. The corroboration model C(n) = 1-(1-p)^n with n=3 gives C(3) ≈ 0.66 for p=0.3 — a 34% chance of missing the true rate entirely.
PROPOSED_FIX: Increase the minimum sample size from 3 to at least 8 (where binomial CI narrows enough to be actionable), or use a Bayesian prior (Beta(1,1)) and require the posterior P(rate < 0.3) > 0.8 before triggering.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F004**
SEVERITY: 0.80
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.70
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `effective_window()` uses `self._pathology_counts.get(detector, 0)` for the `persistent` term, but `_pathology_counts` is keyed inconsistently: sometimes by detector name ("kappa", "mu"), sometimes by composite key ("model_failure_m1", "parser_yield_m2", "dispatch_fp_m1_3"). The `effective_window()` function is only called with detector names ("kappa", "mu") from `record_round()`, but the growth term `(1 + growth * persistent)` reads `_pathology_counts["kappa"]` which is the count for the kappa-stuck pathology specifically. Meanwhile, `_pathology_counts["mu"]` is reset to 0 in the resolution branch of Check 2, but Check 2's diagnosis doesn't set `pathology_key` (per CC2_IM_F013 / DeepSeek_IM_F001). This means `effective_window("mu", ...)` always reads `persistent=0` because the mu pathology count is either never incremented (no `self._pathology_counts["mu"] = persistence + 1` in the mu-increasing branch — the code increments nothing for mu) or is reset. Tracing the code: Check 2's mu-increasing branch does NOT increment `_pathology_counts["mu"]`. It has no `self._pathology_counts["mu"] = persistence + 1` line. So `effective_window("mu", self._mu_increase_window)` always returns `max(2, int(base * decay^resolved * 1))` — the growth term is always 1. The adaptive sensitivity for mu detection is completely non-functional.
PROPOSED_FIX: Add `persistence = self._pathology_counts.get("mu", 0); self._pathology_counts["mu"] = persistence + 1` to the mu-increasing diagnosis branch, mirroring the kappa-stuck branch.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F005**
SEVERITY: 0.78
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.65
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `_extended_p_pass_remediation` convergence check for "no new failures" is structurally broken in a way beyond what CC2_IM_F015 and CC2_IM_F023 identified. The code computes `prev_failures_for_sig = all_failures[:-len(iteration_failures)]` to get failures from previous iterations. But `all_failures` accumulates across ALL iterations via `all_failures.extend(iteration_failures)`. On iteration 1 (index 0), `all_failures` has only iteration 0's failures. On iteration 2 (index 1), `all_failures` has iteration 0 + iteration 1 failures. The slice `all_failures[:-len(iteration_failures)]` removes the LAST N entries (current iteration), leaving all prior. But `current_sigs` is computed from `iteration_failures` (current iteration only), while `prev_sigs` is computed from ALL prior iterations combined. This means a failure that appeared in iteration 0 but not iteration 1 will still be in `prev_sigs` when checking iteration 2, making it appear "not new" even though it re-emerged after being absent. The convergence check should compare consecutive iterations only, not current vs. all-prior-combined.
PROPOSED_FIX: Track `prev_iteration_sigs` as a separate variable updated at the end of each iteration, and compare `current_sigs - prev_iteration_sigs` for the "no new failures" check.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F006**
SEVERITY: 0.75
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.60
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `FailureHandler.get_recovery()` computes `same_type_count` by scanning the ENTIRE `_failure_history` for the model, not just recent history. Combined with the fact that `_record_failure` is called inside `get_recovery` (appending to history AFTER the count is computed), the escalation threshold `n_fail` becomes a lifetime counter. A model that had 2 TIMEOUT failures in round 0-1, recovered and performed well for rounds 2-8, then times out again in round 9, will have `same_type_count = 2` (from the old failures) which equals `n_fail=2`, so `repeated=True`. The recovery action immediately escalates to EXCLUDE instead of giving the model a fresh RETRY. This violates the persistence-window concept used in UNDERPERFORM detection (which correctly windows) but not applied to the escalation logic. Gemini_CDSFL_IM_F001 identified this as "computes repeated by summing ALL historical failures" but was marked severity 0.85 — the finding exists but the prior description didn't trace the interaction with the recovery-after-good-performance scenario.
PROPOSED_FIX: Window `same_type_count` to the last `persistence_window` rounds: `same_type_count = sum(1 for r in history if r.failure_type == failure_type and r.round_idx >= round_idx - self.config.persistence_window)`.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F007**
SEVERITY: 0.73
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.80
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `check_dispatch_health()` appends to `self._diagnoses` directly (line: `self._diagnoses.extend(new_diagnoses)`), bypassing the consolidation point in `record_round()`. CC2_IM_F005 identified this pattern for `record_model_round()`, but `check_dispatch_health()` has the same issue AND an additional problem: it is called from `process_round()` at an unspecified point relative to `record_round()`. If `check_dispatch_health()` runs AFTER `record_round()`, the diagnoses it appends to `self._diagnoses` will not be included in the `new_diagnoses` list returned by `record_round()` for that round. The caller (`process_round()`) may rely on `record_round()`'s return value as the complete set of diagnoses for the round. The dispatch health diagnoses become "orphaned" — present in `self._diagnoses` (and thus in `all_diagnoses`) but never returned to the orchestrator for that round's decision-making. They'll only be visible if someone queries `all_diagnoses` after the fact.
PROPOSED_FIX: Have `check_dispatch_health()` return diagnoses without appending to `self._diagnoses`. The caller should collect all diagnosis sources and append once, or `record_round()` should accept dispatch health data as input and include dispatch diagnoses in its consolidated return.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F008**
SEVERITY: 0.70
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.55
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `self_diagnose()` Self-check 2 (high false positive rate) adjusts `self._sensitivity_decay` upward (from 0.8 toward 0.95), but `effective_window()` uses `decay^resolved` where `decay = self._sensitivity_decay`. Increasing `decay` from 0.8 to 0.85 means `0.85^resolved` > `0.8^resolved` for all `resolved > 0`. This makes the effective window LARGER (less sensitive) for pathologies with resolved history, which is the correct direction for reducing false positives. However, the adjustment also affects pathologies that have NEVER been resolved (`resolved=0`): `decay^0 = 1.0` regardless of decay value. So the self-check 2 adjustment has ZERO effect on pathologies that have never naturally resolved — precisely the pathologies that are NOT false positives. The adjustment only changes sensitivity for pathologies that have resolved before (which are the ones already being handled correctly by the adaptive mechanism). The self-correction is a no-op for the pathologies it most needs to affect: persistent true positives being over-detected.
PROPOSED_FIX: Self-check 2 should also increase the base window parameters (`_stuck_window`, `_mu_increase_window`) by 1, not just `_sensitivity_decay`. Alternatively, introduce a separate `_base_sensitivity_multiplier` that applies regardless of resolution history.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F009**
SEVERITY: 0.68
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.60
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `record_round()` Check 4 (findings decline) requires `all(recent_3[i] < recent_3[i - 1] for i in range(1, len(recent_3)))` — strict monotonic decline over 3 rounds. But the resolution condition checks `recent_3[-1] >= recent_3[0]` — latest >= earliest. These use different windows: the decline check uses `self._finding_counts[-3:]` (last 3 entries), but the resolution check uses the SAME `recent_3` variable. The asymmetry is: decline requires STRICT monotonic decrease across all 3 consecutive values, but resolution only requires the last value to be >= the first value. A sequence like [10, 5, 3, 4] would trigger decline on [10, 5, 3], then on the next round with [5, 3, 4], the decline check fails (4 > 3), and the resolution check sees `recent_3 = [5, 3, 4]` where `4 < 5`, so resolution does NOT fire. The pathology count stays elevated but no new diagnosis is emitted. The pathology is in limbo: not actively declining, not resolved, but `_pathology_counts["findings_decline"]` remains non-zero, inflating the `persistent` term in `effective_window()` for any future decline detection.
PROPOSED_FIX: Reset `_pathology_counts["findings_decline"]` when the strict decline condition is no longer met, regardless of whether the recovery condition is satisfied. The recovery condition should only gate `_resolved_counts` increment and `record_natural_resolution()`.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F010**
SEVERITY: 0.65
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.70
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `FailureHandler.get_recovery()` returns `RecoveryAction.DOWNGRADE_ROLE` for repeated UNDERPERFORM, and the subsequent role mutation only handles `COL → PAR` (per CC2_IM_F024). But the deeper correctness issue is that `DOWNGRADE_ROLE` is applied without checking whether the model is the ONLY model in that role. If the underperforming model is the sole COL and gets downgraded to PAR, there is no COL in the system. The `RoleAssignment` class (outside boundary but consumed by immune layer) is never notified of this change (per CC2_IM_F008), so it doesn't trigger COL re-election. The system continues operating with `role_map` showing no COL, which means `_expected_performance()` for all models uses `b_par` (since `get_baseline(Role.PAR)` is the fallback), flattening the performance baseline and making UNDERPERFORM detection less discriminating. This is a silent degradation of the immune layer's own detection capability caused by its own remediation action.
PROPOSED_FIX: Before executing DOWNGRADE_ROLE, check if the model is the sole holder of its current role. If so, either (a) trigger COL re-election via `RoleAssignment`, or (b) downgrade to LOG_ONLY instead of DOWNGRADE_ROLE to preserve role coverage.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F011**
SEVERITY: 0.62
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.50
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `_standard_p_pass_remediation` Check 2 (natural trend) uses different "improving" definitions for mu vs. other metrics, but the direction logic for non-mu metrics is wrong for `finding_count`. The check `recent_3[i] >= recent_3[i - 1] * 0.95` considers a 5% decline as "improving." For finding counts, a sequence [10, 9.5, 9.0] (each 5% lower) would pass the "improving" check, causing the P-pass to SKIP the remediation. But finding counts declining by 5% per round is NOT improvement — it's the exact pathology that `findings_decline` is trying to remediate. The 0.95 multiplier was designed for metrics like kappa where small fluctuations are noise, but for integer-valued finding counts, a consistent 5% decline over 3 rounds is a meaningful signal. The P-pass incorrectly blocks remediation for the pathology it's supposed to fix.
PROPOSED_FIX: Use metric-specific improvement thresholds: for `finding_count`, require `recent_3[i] >= recent_3[i-1]` (non-declining). For `kappa` and `novelty`, the 0.95 tolerance is appropriate.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F012**
SEVERITY: 0.58
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.45
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `record_model_round()` monotonic decline detection uses `recent_3[0] > recent_3[1] > recent_3[2]` (strict inequality) with a noise filter of `total_decline >= 3`. But for models that produce few findings per round (e.g., 3→2→1), the decline is real and significant (67% drop) yet `total_decline = 2` which is below the threshold. Meanwhile, a model going from 100→97→94 has `total_decline = 6` and triggers the detection, even though the percentage decline (6%) is negligible. The noise filter uses an absolute threshold on an unbounded metric, making it over-sensitive for high-output models and under-sensitive for low-output models. The system-wide Check 4 has the same issue (threshold of 5) but CC2_IM_F010 only noted the small-pool problem, not the asymmetric sensitivity.
PROPOSED_FIX: Use a relative threshold: `total_decline / recent_3[0] >= 0.3` (30% decline from peak) instead of `total_decline >= 3`.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F013**
SEVERITY: 0.55
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.40
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `CorrelatedFailureModel.pairwise_joint_failure()` uses the formula `P(i,j) = p_i * p_j + v_ij * min(p_i, p_j) * (1 - max(p_i, p_j))` and then clamps to `min(p_i, p_j)`. But the formula can produce values LESS than `p_i * p_j` (the independent baseline) when `v_ij` is negative — except `set_vulnerability` enforces `v_ij >= 0`. The real issue is that the formula doesn't reduce to the correct Fréchet upper bound. When `v_ij = 1.0` (perfectly correlated), the formula gives `p_i * p_j + min(p_i, p_j) * (1 - max(p_i, p_j))`. For `p_i = p_j = p`, this is `p² + p(1-p) = p`, which is correct. But for `p_i = 0.9, p_j = 0.1`, it gives `0.09 + 0.1 * 0.1 = 0.1 = min(0.9, 0.1)`, which is correct. However, for `p_i = 0.5, p_j = 0.3, v_ij = 1.0`, it gives `0.15 + 0.3 * 0.5 = 0.30 = min(0.5, 0.3)` — correct. The formula is actually well-behaved for the pairwise case. The real bug is in `correlated_class_failure` which uses `p_min` instead of the actual `p_i, p_j` values (per Gemini_IM_F004), AND takes `max(independent_all, max_pairwise_joint)` which conflates a pairwise probability with an all-fail probability (per CC2_IM_F016). But there's an additional issue: the final clamp `min(result, min_individual)` can produce a value LOWER than `independent_all` when `min_individual < independent_all`. For 4 models with rates [0.01, 0.9, 0.9, 0.9], `independent_all = 0.01 * 0.729 ≈ 0.00729`, but `min_individual = 0.01`, so the clamp doesn't bite. For [0.001, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5], `independent_all = 0.000125`, `min_individual = 0.001`, fine. The clamp is actually never binding when `independent_all` is the max — it only bites when `max_pairwise_joint > min_individual`, which can happen when two high-rate models have high vulnerability but a third model has a very low rate. In that case, the function returns `min_individual` which is correct as an upper bound but may be a gross overestimate.
PROPOSED_FIX: Replace the `max(independent_all, max_pairwise_joint)` heuristic with a proper inclusion-exclusion bound or Fréchet bound for N models. For N=3: `P(A∩B∩C) <= min(P(A∩B), P(A∩C), P(B∩C))` using the pairwise joints already computed.
VERIFIED: TRUE

**FINDING_ID: IM_F014**
SEVERITY: 0.52
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.35
VERIFIED: TRUE
DESCRIPTION: `record_model_round()` cost-per-finding spike detection excludes the current round from `cpf_history` (using `times[:-1]` and `findings_hist[:-1]`), which is correct for computing historical statistics. But it requires `len(times) >= 3`, meaning the model must have had at least 3 rounds of data (including current). The first spike can only be detected on round 2 (0-indexed), and only if rounds 0 and 1 both had `f > 0 and t > 0`. For a model that times out in round 0 (f=0), produces findings in rounds 1-2, the `cpf_history` on round 2 has only 1 entry (round 1), which fails the `len(cpf_history) >= 2` check. The spike detection is effectively disabled until round 3 for any model that had a single bad round early on. In a 5-round protocol, this means 60% of the protocol may pass before spike detection activates.
PROPOSED_FIX: Reduce the minimum history requirement to `len(cpf_history) >= 1` and use a fixed threshold (e.g., 3× the single historical CPF) when only one data point is available, falling back to the 2σ method when sufficient data exists.
VERIFIED: TRUE
